Pregnancy

Iron-deficiency anaemia before, during and after pregnancy

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Iron deficiency can start before pregnancy, become more apparent as pregnancy increases iron needs, or persist after blood loss at birth. It can cause anaemia, but tiredness or a low haemoglobin result does not automatically mean that iron is the cause. A useful plan identifies the reason, chooses suitable replacement when needed and checks the response. Care continues after birth; you do not have to accept ongoing exhaustion as an unavoidable part of parenting.

Low iron and anaemia are related, but different

Iron helps the body make haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen. Iron deficiency means that available iron or stored iron is insufficient. Anaemia means that haemoglobin is below the appropriate threshold. Stores can become depleted before anaemia develops, and anaemia can also have other causes. A blood count and, when appropriate, tests such as ferritin help the clinician work out which problem is present.

Ferritin reflects iron stores, but inflammation can raise it and make an apparently reassuring result harder to interpret. Haemoglobin also changes with the stage of pregnancy. Thresholds and testing pathways differ between guidelines and clinical circumstances; neither a laboratory flag nor a single ferritin number should be interpreted alone. The team may consider symptoms, bleeding, inflammation, previous results and other tests before deciding on treatment.

Symptoms need assessment, rather than self-diagnosis

Iron-deficiency anaemia may cause tiredness, weakness, headaches, paler skin, dizziness, cold hands or feet, breathlessness or noticeable heartbeats. Some people notice brittle nails or other changes, while others have few symptoms. These features are not specific to iron deficiency. Feeling unusually cold, for example, is not a substitute for a measured temperature or a blood test.

Tell the clinician about symptoms, their onset and how they affect ordinary activity. New chest pain, breathing difficulty, fainting or persistent rapid heartbeats need assessment for other potentially serious causes; do not assume that they will resolve with an iron tablet. Seek urgent or emergency help according to the warning signs below, even if you already have a diagnosis of anaemia.

Find the cause before conception when possible

Low intake, heavy periods, other blood loss and difficulty absorbing iron can contribute to deficiency. Conditions such as coeliac disease or Crohn’s disease may affect absorption. Previous pregnancy, a history of anaemia, dietary restrictions and medicines are also useful parts of the history. Heavy periods deserve assessment and a plan for the bleeding as well as replacement of lost iron.

If you are planning pregnancy and have symptoms, a previous low result or a known risk, ask about testing and treatment before conception. Anaemia may involve vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, a haemoglobin disorder such as thalassaemia or sickle cell disease, inflammation or another condition. The clinician may investigate more than one cause. Do not keep increasing iron yourself when the diagnosis or response is unclear.

Why pregnancy changes the picture

Pregnancy requires iron for the expanding red-cell mass and the developing pregnancy. Plasma, the liquid part of blood, increases more than red-cell mass, so haemoglobin concentration normally falls to some extent. This is not the same as saying that blood volume doubles or that every lower haemoglobin result is harmless dilution. Someone who starts pregnancy with depleted stores has less reserve as needs rise.

Blood-count testing is commonly offered early in pregnancy and repeated later, with extra tests when symptoms, risk or treatment require them. For example, the UK NICE routine pathway includes a blood count at the first face-to-face antenatal appointment and at 28 weeks. Other countries and individual situations use different schedules. Ask when your own next test is due rather than assuming that every trimester requires the same tests or that one normal early test settles the question.

What anaemia can mean for pregnancy and birth

Anaemia reduces the reserve available to cope with blood loss at birth and may increase the likelihood of needing additional treatment, including transfusion in some circumstances. Studies associate maternal anaemia with outcomes such as preterm birth, lower birth weight and other maternal or newborn complications. Severe anaemia is particularly concerning. These are population associations, not a prediction that a particular pregnancy will have a poor outcome.

Reports also describe associations with pre-eclampsia and maternal or perinatal death, but anaemia has several causes and is influenced by illness, nutrition, bleeding and access to care. It is not sound to promise that taking iron will prevent each of these outcomes. The practical aim is to diagnose the problem, treat confirmed deficiency appropriately, review the response and plan care around the person’s circumstances. A low result is a health issue to support, not a reason for blame.

Use food to support iron intake safely

Iron-containing foods include properly cooked meat, poultry or fish, and plant foods such as beans, lentils, iron-fortified cereals, leafy vegetables, seeds and other suitable foods. Animal and plant iron are absorbed differently; vitamin-C-containing food alongside a plant source can help its absorption. Shellfish are an animal food, not a plant source, and pregnancy food-safety advice still applies. Avoid raw or undercooked shellfish and follow local advice about suitable fish and preparation.

A varied diet supports treatment, but food alone may not replace enough iron once iron-deficiency anaemia is established. Do not use liver or liver products as a pregnancy anaemia remedy: their high vitamin A content is a concern. Avoid supplements containing retinol unless specifically advised by the treating team. A dietitian can help if nausea, a restricted diet, food access or digestive illness makes eating difficult; needing support is not a personal failure.

Separate nutritional needs, prevention and treatment

The US recommended dietary allowance during pregnancy is 27 mg of iron per day. That is a nutritional reference, not a universal dose for treating anaemia. Public-health prevention programmes also differ: WHO recommends a particular daily iron and folic acid regimen in antenatal care, with alternatives only in defined circumstances. A prenatal vitamin, a prevention programme and treatment of diagnosed deficiency serve different purposes.

Check the actual product and the amount of elemental iron, rather than comparing tablet weights alone. The iron salt printed on a packet is not the same amount as elemental iron. Ask which prenatal supplement and iron medicine to take, how often and for how long; some prenatal products contain little or no iron. Do not automatically add products together, double a dose or change a whole prenatal vitamin to alternate days because you have heard that some iron treatments use that schedule.

Take oral iron in a way you can tolerate

Oral iron is commonly used when replacement is needed and it is suitable for the individual. The clinician chooses the product and schedule. Some people are advised to use a lower dose or an alternate-day iron regimen when tolerability is a problem; this is a treatment decision, not a rule for everyone. Nausea, stomach discomfort, constipation and darker stools can occur. Tell the team about troublesome effects rather than stopping silently or repeatedly taking extra tablets.

Iron is often absorbed better on an empty stomach, but taking it with food may be advised if stomach effects make treatment difficult. Water is suitable; acidic juice, including grapefruit juice, is not required. Follow the product instructions and ask a pharmacist about spacing from tea, coffee, dairy products, other supplements and medicines. Some medicines, including levothyroxine, antacids and certain antibiotics, need individualized timing. Avoid a blanket food ban or one timing rule for every medicine.

Check whether treatment is working

Agree a date for repeat testing and what improvement the team expects. Some pregnancy pathways recheck haemoglobin after about two to three weeks of oral treatment, with timing adjusted to symptoms, the starting result and gestation. Feeling somewhat better does not prove that stores have recovered, and a blood result that has not improved needs review rather than an automatic higher dose.

The team can check the diagnosis, dose and administration, missed doses, tolerability, absorption, continuing blood loss and possible additional causes of anaemia. Explain what is realistically happening with the medicine so the plan can be adapted. Treatment often continues after haemoglobin normalizes to replenish stores, sometimes for months and into the postpartum period. Follow the agreed course and repeat-test plan rather than stopping solely because pregnancy has ended or symptoms have eased.

When IV iron or transfusion may be considered

Intravenous iron may be considered for confirmed iron deficiency when oral iron cannot be used or tolerated, has not worked despite appropriate review, or more rapid correction is needed. Timing, severity, proximity to birth, symptoms and the exact product matter. It is generally considered after the first trimester when benefits outweigh risks. Being in the third trimester does not by itself mean that an infusion is necessary.

IV iron needs a service able to recognize and treat reactions, with appropriate observation. Discuss the expected benefit, possible hypersensitivity, product-specific effects such as low phosphate, and the risk of skin staining if iron leaks outside the vein. A transfusion is a different treatment. Decisions about it depend on bleeding, symptoms, circulatory stability, urgency and the whole clinical picture, rather than a haemoglobin number alone. Severe symptoms or active major bleeding should not wait for a routine infusion appointment.

Make a birth and early recovery plan

Tell the maternity team about ongoing anaemia, recent blood results, treatment and any difficulty taking it. They may review the place of birth and measures to anticipate or manage blood loss, especially when anaemia is substantial. Anaemia does not automatically require induction or caesarean birth; the plan depends on obstetric indications and the individual’s condition.

After birth, previous anaemia, significant blood loss or symptoms may lead to an early haemoglobin check and further treatment. Ferritin can be raised by inflammation soon after birth, so a result at that time may not reliably show iron stores. The team may instead consider the blood count, bleeding history, examination and later follow-up. Ask who will review the results after discharge, when to repeat tests and whom to contact if symptoms worsen.

Postpartum anaemia can persist

Low stores carried into birth and blood loss during delivery can leave iron-deficiency anaemia after pregnancy. Reduced or absent periods during breastfeeding do not automatically restore those stores, and periods do not follow the same pattern for everyone. Continued tiredness, weakness, dizziness or palpitations should not simply be attributed to feeding, sleep loss or being a new parent.

A stable person may continue prescribed oral iron; selected circumstances require IV treatment or other urgent care. Postpartum prevention recommendations for some populations are not a substitute for an individualized treatment course when anaemia is already present. Arrange the follow-up, manage ongoing bleeding and ask for practical help with meals, medicine and appointments. Sudden or very heavy vaginal bleeding, especially with faintness or a rapid heartbeat, needs immediate emergency assessment rather than an iron adjustment.

Support feeding, mood and everyday recovery

Prescribed oral ferrous sulfate is usually compatible with breastfeeding. If a different product or an infusion is proposed, confirm its specific advice with the team. Treating the parent does not treat an infant’s iron deficiency; a baby who needs assessment or supplementation needs their own plan. Anaemia-related exhaustion can make feeding and daily tasks harder, but feeding choices and the need for help do not measure the quality of the parent–baby relationship.

Postpartum anaemia has been associated with fatigue and mood symptoms, but depression, anxiety and difficulty coping need assessment in their own right. Iron is not a guaranteed way to prevent depression or improve attachment, and it must not replace mental-health support. Ask for help promptly if your mood or ability to cope is deteriorating. Serious self-injury, an overdose or being unable to keep yourself or someone else safe requires immediate local emergency help.

Know which symptoms need emergency care

Seek local emergency help for sudden breathing difficulty; severe difficulty breathing, gasping or inability to get words out; chest or upper-back pain; a tight or heavy chest; pain spreading to an arm, back, neck or jaw; very pale, blue or grey skin or lips; sudden confusion; fainting or loss of consciousness; or a very fast heartbeat. Ongoing palpitations that do not go away also need emergency assessment, as do palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness, feeling faint or fainting. These are alternative warning signs, not a list that must all be present. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask someone else to take you or arrange an ambulance.

Seek urgent clinical advice about new or worsening breathlessness, coughing up blood, one-sided leg pain or swelling, or a worrying episode that has stopped. After birth, fever with a painful or tender abdomen, or a headache with visual changes or vomiting, also needs immediate clinical advice. Tell the service that you are pregnant or have recently given birth. Anaemia must not be used to explain away a possible blood clot, infection, pregnancy complication or another emergency.

Keep iron medicines safe

Keep all iron medicines and supplements out of children’s sight and reach, in their original packaging. Too much iron can be dangerous, particularly for a child. If anyone takes more than prescribed, or a child swallows iron that was not prescribed for them, seek immediate medical or poison-service advice even before symptoms appear. Do not take extra tablets to correct a result more quickly or make up a missed dose by doubling it.

Suspected poisoning needs emergency assessment. While waiting for medical advice, do not induce vomiting or give food or drink. Keep the packet and details of what was taken available without delaying help. Someone who is unresponsive, has breathing difficulty or has a seizure needs local emergency services immediately. The affected person must not drive to emergency care; arrange another driver or an ambulance.

Leave with a clear plan for all three stages

Before conception, ask what caused the deficiency and whether bleeding or an absorption problem needs treatment. During pregnancy, confirm the test schedule, exact medicine, elemental dose, timing and response review. Before discharge after birth, agree how long to continue treatment and who will repeat and review the blood tests. A plan should be practical enough to use alongside nausea, constipation, feeding and limited sleep.

Bring a list of medicines and supplements, previous results, symptoms and any missed or difficult doses. Ask what would change the plan to an infusion or another investigation, and what symptoms mean you should seek help before the next appointment. Food, treatment and practical support can work together, but neither a dietary improvement nor a supplement should delay assessment of serious or persistent symptoms.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Ask what the blood count and iron tests show, what may have caused the problem and when the response will be checked. Mention heavy periods, birth blood loss, digestive illness and any worsening symptoms.

Confirm the exact product, elemental iron amount, schedule, medicine and food spacing, and what to do about side effects or missed doses. Ask before combining supplements or changing to alternate-day treatment.

Before birth or discharge, agree the ongoing treatment, repeat-test date and review contact. Arrange practical feeding, food and mental-health support, and know the urgent and emergency routes without waiting to finish a symptom record.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you organize a symptom timeline, prescribed-medicine reminders, appointments and questions for your care team. It cannot diagnose the cause of anaemia, interpret a blood result as an all-clear, choose a dose or infusion, or replace maternity or emergency assessment. Do not delay contact while recording information.

When to seek help

Seek local emergency help for sudden breathing difficulty, severe breathing trouble, chest or upper-back pain, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to the arm/back/neck/jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion, fainting or loss of consciousness, a very fast heartbeat, or ongoing palpitations that do not settle. Palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness are also emergency warnings. Sudden or very heavy postpartum vaginal bleeding needs immediate emergency assessment. The signs are alternative triggers; do not wait for all to occur. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. New or worsening breathlessness, coughing blood, one-sided leg pain or swelling, postpartum fever with abdominal tenderness, or headache with visual changes/vomiting needs immediate clinical advice. Taking extra iron or a child swallowing it needs immediate medical or poison-service advice; suspected poisoning requires emergency assessment, without inducing vomiting or giving food or drink while waiting. Serious self-injury, overdose or inability to keep anyone safe also requires immediate emergency help.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Iron deficiency may exist before anaemia, and not every low haemoglobin result is caused by low iron; diagnosis includes the cause and clinical context.
  • Start assessment before pregnancy when possible, follow the local antenatal testing plan and arrange postpartum review after blood loss or ongoing symptoms.
  • Dietary needs, prevention supplements and treatment doses are different; use the exact prescribed product and check the elemental iron amount and medicine timing.
  • Review response and tolerability before changing treatment. IV iron is selected care, and the third trimester alone does not make it necessary.
  • Persistent postpartum symptoms deserve support. Emergency chest, breathing, bleeding or consciousness changes and suspected iron poisoning must not wait for routine anaemia follow-up.

Frequently asked questions

What is iron-deficiency anaemia?

It is anaemia caused by insufficient iron for normal haemoglobin production. Iron deficiency can also occur before haemoglobin becomes low. A blood count, appropriate iron tests and assessment of the cause help distinguish it from other anaemias, including B12 or folate deficiency, haemoglobin disorders and illness-related anaemia. Ferritin can be misleading when inflammation is present, so do not interpret one result alone.

What symptoms can it cause?

Possible symptoms include tiredness, weakness, paler skin, headaches, dizziness, cold hands or feet, brittle nails, breathlessness and noticeable heartbeats. Symptoms are not specific enough to diagnose iron deficiency. New chest pain, sudden breathing difficulty, fainting, a very fast heartbeat or ongoing palpitations that do not settle need emergency assessment; do not wait for iron to help.

Why is iron important during pregnancy?

Iron supports haemoglobin production as the red-cell mass and the developing pregnancy’s needs increase. Adequate stores also help preserve reserve for blood loss at birth. Plasma expands more than red-cell mass, so some fall in haemoglobin concentration is physiological, but this does not make every low result normal. Testing, appropriate food and prescribed replacement when needed work together; pregnancy does not simply double the person’s blood volume.

Can iron-deficiency anaemia affect the baby?

Maternal anaemia is associated with outcomes including preterm birth and low birth weight, with particular concern when it is severe. Other maternal and newborn complications are also reported, but the causes and circumstances vary. These associations are not a prediction for one baby, and iron treatment cannot be promised to prevent every complication. Diagnose the cause, treat confirmed deficiency and follow the maternity team’s plan without blame.

What should I do before trying to conceive?

Ask about assessment if you have symptoms, heavy periods, previous anaemia, a restricted diet or a condition that affects absorption. Treatment should address the cause as well as the iron deficit. Bring previous results and all medicines or supplements. Do not assume that every anaemia is iron deficiency or keep increasing an iron dose without review.

Does poor response to tablets mean I need IV iron?

Not automatically. The team should review the diagnosis, product, administration, tolerability, absorption, continuing blood loss and other causes, then check the response on an agreed schedule. IV iron may be appropriate if oral treatment cannot be used or has not worked, or if faster correction is needed, generally after the first trimester following a risk–benefit assessment. It needs a suitable monitored service; being in the third trimester alone is not an indication.

Will breastfeeding or the end of pregnancy cure the anaemia?

No. Blood loss and low stores can leave anaemia after birth, even if periods are absent. Continue the prescribed plan and arrange follow-up rather than stopping because the baby has been born. Oral ferrous sulfate is usually compatible with breastfeeding, but the baby’s iron needs require a separate assessment. Fatigue and mood problems deserve help in their own right; treatment is not a test of parenting or a guaranteed cure for depression.

When should I seek urgent or emergency help?

Use local emergency services for sudden breathing difficulty, severe breathing trouble, chest or upper-back pain, a tight or heavy chest, pain spreading to the arm, back, neck or jaw, very pale/blue/grey skin or lips, sudden confusion, fainting, a very fast heartbeat, or ongoing palpitations that do not settle. Palpitations with chest pain, breathlessness or faintness also require emergency assessment. Sudden or very heavy postpartum vaginal bleeding needs immediate emergency help. These are independent alternatives; do not wait for all of them. Do not drive yourself; arrange another driver or an ambulance. New or worsening breathlessness, coughing blood, one-sided leg pain or swelling, or postpartum fever with abdominal tenderness or headache with visual changes/vomiting needs immediate clinical advice. Extra iron ingestion needs immediate medical or poison-service advice; suspected poisoning needs emergency assessment without inducing vomiting or giving food or drink while waiting.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
